# Exercise 2.4 — Leakage {#sec-leakage}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- State which preprocessing steps are *fitted* to data and which are not, and
  explain why only the fitted ones can leak.
- Build the same impute-and-scale pipeline twice, once leaking and once not,
  and report the difference in test MAE as a number you computed.
- Say which kinds of leakage cost you nothing and which destroy the
  evaluation, with an example of each.
:::

## Why this, here

Everything you did today was fitted to the whole file. The median that filled
the gaps in @sec-missing-data was computed from all 200 patients; the mean and
standard deviation in @sec-transforming came from all 345. On Day 1 you learned
to hold rows back so that the evaluation means something (@sec-pipeline). Those
two habits are in direct conflict, and this exercise is about which one wins.

The rule is short: **anything learned from data is part of the model, and must
be learned from the training rows only.** A log is not learned. A mean is. So
is a median, a standard deviation, a minimum, a set of category levels, an
imputation model, and the choice of which predictors to keep.

## Today's regression

Predict body mass index from the measurements that relate to it: skin-fold
thickness, blood pressure, age and number of pregnancies. `triceps` is missing
in about a third of rows, so imputation is unavoidable, which is the point.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)
tidymodels_prefer()

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dia <- diabetes |>
  mutate(across(c(glucose, pressure, triceps, insulin, mass), ~ na_if(.x, 0))) |>
  filter(!is.na(mass)) |>                 # the outcome must be present
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>        # so we can line rows up again later
  select(row_id, mass, triceps, pressure, age, pregnant, glucose)

nrow(dia)
colSums(is.na(dia))
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
dia = diabetes.copy()
impossible = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
dia[impossible] = dia[impossible].replace(0, np.nan)
dia = dia.dropna(subset=["mass"])[
    ["mass", "triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant", "glucose"]]

print(len(dia))
print(dia.isna().sum())
```
:::

And the split, made once and used for everything that follows.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

mae_baseline <- mean(abs(test$mass - mean(train$mass)))
mae_baseline
```

## Python

```{python}
train, test = train_test_split(dia, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
print(len(train), len(test))

mae_baseline = np.abs(test["mass"] - train["mass"].mean()).mean()
print(mae_baseline)
```
:::

A model that predicts the training mean BMI for everybody is wrong by between
five and six BMI units. Everything below has to beat that to be worth running.

## Leak 1 — Scaling before the split

The textbook mistake. Standardise the predictors using the mean and standard
deviation of all 755 rows, then split, then fit. Compare with standardising
using the training rows only. For both, fill the gaps the same way, so that the
only difference is where the scaling constants came from.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
preds <- c("triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant")
fill_na <- function(df, values) {
  for (v in names(values)) df[[v]][is.na(df[[v]])] <- values[[v]]
  df
}
train_means <- lapply(train[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
train_f <- fill_na(train, train_means)
test_f  <- fill_na(test,  train_means)

# WRONG: centre and scale using every row, training and test together
all_f  <- fill_na(dia, train_means)
mu_all <- sapply(all_f[preds], mean); sd_all <- sapply(all_f[preds], sd)
scale_by <- function(df, mu, sd) {
  for (v in names(mu)) df[[v]] <- (df[[v]] - mu[[v]]) / sd[[v]]
  df
}
model_formula <- mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant
fit_leak  <- lm(model_formula, data = scale_by(train_f, mu_all, sd_all))
mae_scale_leak <- mean(abs(test_f$mass -
  predict(fit_leak, scale_by(test_f, mu_all, sd_all))))

# RIGHT: constants from the training rows only
mu_tr <- sapply(train_f[preds], mean); sd_tr <- sapply(train_f[preds], sd)
fit_ok <- lm(model_formula, data = scale_by(train_f, mu_tr, sd_tr))
mae_scale_ok <- mean(abs(test_f$mass -
  predict(fit_ok, scale_by(test_f, mu_tr, sd_tr))))

c(leaky = mae_scale_leak, honest = mae_scale_ok,
  difference = mae_scale_leak - mae_scale_ok)
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

preds = ["triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant"]
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(train[preds])
train_f = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(train[preds]), columns=preds, index=train.index)
test_f  = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(test[preds]),  columns=preds, index=test.index)
all_f   = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(dia[preds]),   columns=preds, index=dia.index)

# WRONG: scaler fitted on every row, training and test together
sc_leak = StandardScaler().fit(all_f)
fit_leak = LinearRegression().fit(sc_leak.transform(train_f), train["mass"])
mae_scale_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_leak.predict(sc_leak.transform(test_f)))

# RIGHT: scaler fitted on the training rows only
sc_ok = StandardScaler().fit(train_f)
fit_ok = LinearRegression().fit(sc_ok.transform(train_f), train["mass"])
mae_scale_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_ok.predict(sc_ok.transform(test_f)))

print(mae_scale_leak, mae_scale_ok, mae_scale_leak - mae_scale_ok)
```
:::

The two MAEs are the same number, and not approximately: they agree to the
last decimal place the computer keeps, and the difference printed is
floating-point arithmetic rather than statistics. This is not a near miss. It
is an identity.

Standardisation subtracts a constant and divides by another. Ordinary least
squares then estimates whatever coefficients undo that, exactly: scale a
predictor by $c$ and its coefficient becomes $\beta/c$, so every fitted value
is unchanged. The leak transferred information — the test rows did influence
$\mu$ and $\sigma$ — and the model had no way to use it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not conclude that scaling leakage is harmless
It is harmless *here*, because the model is linear and the leak is an affine
transformation. Put a penalty on the coefficients, as ridge and lasso do, and
the scale decides how hard each coefficient is pushed towards zero, so the leak
changes the fit. Use a distance-based method and it changes the neighbours. The
rule exists because you cannot audit, at the moment you write the
preprocessing, every model that will later be fitted on top of it.
:::

## Task 1 — Leak 2: imputation before the split

Now the leak the original version of this material was most worried about. Fill
the missing `triceps` and `pressure` with the mean of **all 755 rows**, then
split and fit; then do it again with the mean of the training rows only. Report
both MAEs and the difference.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
global_means <- lapply(dia[preds], mean, na.rm = ______)      # all rows: the leak
train_means  <- lapply(train[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)

c(global_triceps = global_means$triceps, train_triceps = train_means$triceps)

fit_g <- lm(model_formula, data = fill_na(train, ______))
mae_imp_leak <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_g, fill_na(test, global_means))))

fit_t <- lm(model_formula, data = fill_na(train, train_means))
mae_imp_ok <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_t, fill_na(test, train_means))))

c(leaky = mae_imp_leak, honest = mae_imp_ok, difference = mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
c(model = mae_imp_ok, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`fill_na()` is defined above and takes a data frame and a named list of
replacement values. The leaky version differs from the honest one by one
argument: which frame the means were computed from.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
global_means <- lapply(dia[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)        # all rows: the leak
train_means  <- lapply(train[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)

c(global_triceps = global_means$triceps, train_triceps = train_means$triceps)

fit_g <- lm(model_formula, data = fill_na(train, global_means))
mae_imp_leak <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_g, fill_na(test, global_means))))

fit_t <- lm(model_formula, data = fill_na(train, train_means))
mae_imp_ok <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_t, fill_na(test, train_means))))

c(leaky = mae_imp_leak, honest = mae_imp_ok, difference = mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
c(model = mae_imp_ok, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
imp_leak = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(______[preds])   # all rows: the leak
imp_ok   = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(train[preds])

print(imp_leak.statistics_[0], imp_ok.statistics_[0])          # imputed triceps

fit_g = LinearRegression().fit(imp_leak.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_g.predict(imp_leak.transform(test[preds])))

fit_t = LinearRegression().fit(imp_ok.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_t.predict(imp_ok.transform(test[preds])))

print(mae_imp_leak, mae_imp_ok, mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
print(mae_imp_ok, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
imp_leak = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(dia[preds])      # all rows: the leak
imp_ok   = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(train[preds])

print(imp_leak.statistics_[0], imp_ok.statistics_[0])          # imputed triceps

fit_g = LinearRegression().fit(imp_leak.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_g.predict(imp_leak.transform(test[preds])))

fit_t = LinearRegression().fit(imp_ok.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_t.predict(imp_ok.transform(test[preds])))

print(mae_imp_leak, mae_imp_ok, mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
print(mae_imp_ok, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)
```
:::
:::
:::

This time the two numbers genuinely differ, because the imputed constant is
data the model consumes rather than a rescaling it can absorb. They differ
around the fourth decimal place of a quantity measured in BMI units, and which
of them is larger depends on the split. The leak is real and it is worth
nothing: a mean over 604 rows and a mean over 755 rows of the same population
are nearly the same number, and the choice between them is not detectable in
any result you would report.

## The result that should bother you

Two leaks, carefully constructed, and the scoreboard is unchanged. If you stop
here you will leave believing that the rule is a formality.

So try a third, and keep everything else the same. Impute the missing
`triceps` and `pressure` by *predicting* them — a sensible thing to do, far
better statistics than the mean — using a regression fitted to all 755 rows
with every other column available to it, **including `mass`, the outcome**.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
# WRONG: an imputation model fitted on all rows, allowed to see the outcome
dia_leak <- dia
for (v in c("triceps", "pressure")) {
  others <- c("mass", "age", "pregnant", "glucose")      # note what is in here
  usable <- complete.cases(dia_leak[others])
  m    <- lm(reformulate(others, v), data = dia_leak[usable & !is.na(dia_leak[[v]]), ])
  miss <- usable & is.na(dia_leak[[v]])
  dia_leak[[v]][miss] <- predict(m, newdata = dia_leak[miss, ])
}
dia_leak <- fill_na(dia_leak, lapply(dia_leak[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))

train_leak <- dia_leak |> filter(row_id %in% train$row_id)
test_leak  <- dia_leak |> filter(row_id %in% test$row_id)

fit_leak3 <- lm(model_formula, data = train_leak)
mae_impmodel_leak <- mean(abs(test_leak$mass - predict(fit_leak3, test_leak)))

# RIGHT: the same idea, fitted on the training rows, outcome withheld
train_ok <- train; test_ok <- test
for (v in c("triceps", "pressure")) {
  others <- c("age", "pregnant", "glucose")              # and what is not
  m <- lm(reformulate(others, v),
          data = train_ok[complete.cases(train_ok[others]) & !is.na(train_ok[[v]]), ])
  for (nm in c("train_ok", "test_ok")) {
    d <- get(nm); miss <- complete.cases(d[others]) & is.na(d[[v]])
    d[[v]][miss] <- predict(m, newdata = d[miss, ]); assign(nm, d)
  }
}
train_ok <- fill_na(train_ok, lapply(train_ok[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))
test_ok  <- fill_na(test_ok,  lapply(train_ok[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))

fit_ok3 <- lm(model_formula, data = train_ok)
mae_impmodel_ok <- mean(abs(test_ok$mass - predict(fit_ok3, test_ok)))

c(leaky = mae_impmodel_leak, honest = mae_impmodel_ok,
  difference = mae_impmodel_leak - mae_impmodel_ok)
```

## Python

```{python}
# WRONG: an imputation model fitted on all rows, allowed to see the outcome
dia_leak = dia.copy()
for v in ["triceps", "pressure"]:
    others = ["mass", "age", "pregnant", "glucose"]
    obs = dia_leak[v].notna() & dia_leak[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    m = LinearRegression().fit(dia_leak.loc[obs, others], dia_leak.loc[obs, v])
    miss = dia_leak[v].isna() & dia_leak[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    dia_leak.loc[miss, v] = m.predict(dia_leak.loc[miss, others])
dia_leak[preds] = dia_leak[preds].fillna(dia_leak[preds].mean())

train_leak, test_leak = dia_leak.loc[train.index], dia_leak.loc[test.index]
fit_leak3 = LinearRegression().fit(train_leak[preds], train_leak["mass"])
mae_impmodel_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test_leak["mass"], fit_leak3.predict(test_leak[preds]))

# RIGHT: the same idea, fitted on the training rows, outcome withheld
train_ok, test_ok = train.copy(), test.copy()
for v in ["triceps", "pressure"]:
    others = ["age", "pregnant", "glucose"]
    obs = train_ok[v].notna() & train_ok[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    m = LinearRegression().fit(train_ok.loc[obs, others], train_ok.loc[obs, v])
    for d in (train_ok, test_ok):
        miss = d[v].isna() & d[others].notna().all(axis=1)
        d.loc[miss, v] = m.predict(d.loc[miss, others])
train_ok[preds] = train_ok[preds].fillna(train_ok[preds].mean())
test_ok[preds]  = test_ok[preds].fillna(train_ok[preds].mean())

fit_ok3 = LinearRegression().fit(train_ok[preds], train_ok["mass"])
mae_impmodel_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test_ok["mass"], fit_ok3.predict(test_ok[preds]))

print(mae_impmodel_leak, mae_impmodel_ok, mae_impmodel_leak - mae_impmodel_ok)
```
:::

Now the number moves, by around half a BMI unit, and in the flattering
direction. Over sixty different splits the leaky version won every single
time, by between 0.3 and 0.8 units.

1. The imputation model learned `triceps` as a function of `mass`. Every
   imputed `triceps` in the test set is therefore a coded copy of that
   patient's own BMI — the thing you are about to predict.
2. The outcome model then "discovers" that `triceps` predicts `mass` very well
   in exactly those rows, and the test MAE improves. Nothing was fabricated;
   the arithmetic is correct throughout. The test set simply stopped being
   held out.
3. This is why the rule is about information rather than about code order.
   Leak 1 moved a statistic across the split and cost nothing. Leak 3 moved
   the *outcome* across it, through a column that does not look like an
   outcome, and cost the entire evaluation.

The difference between leaks 2 and 3 is not how careless the analyst was. It is
how much row-specific information the fitted step could carry. A mean carries
almost none. A model carries as much as you let it.

## Task 2 — The leak-free pipeline, written once

Doing this by hand is how the mistakes get made, which is why both languages
have a way to package preprocessing and model into one object that can only be
fitted on what it is given.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rec <- recipe(mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant, data = ______) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"))

final <- last_fit(wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(mae))
mae_pipeline <- collect_metrics(final)$.estimate
mae_pipeline
c(model = mae_pipeline, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A recipe is declared against the frame whose *structure* it should learn from,
and `last_fit()` then re-estimates every step on the training half of the split
you hand it. Giving the recipe the test rows at this point would undo the thing
you are demonstrating.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
rec <- recipe(mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant, data = train) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"))

final <- last_fit(wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(mae))
mae_pipeline <- collect_metrics(final)$.estimate
mae_pipeline
c(model = mae_pipeline, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")),
                    ("scale", StandardScaler())])
prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, preds)])
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("model", LinearRegression())])

pipe.fit(______[preds], ______["mass"])
mae_pipeline = mean_absolute_error(test["mass"], pipe.predict(test[preds]))
print(mae_pipeline)
print(mae_pipeline, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")),
                    ("scale", StandardScaler())])
prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, preds)])
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("model", LinearRegression())])

pipe.fit(train[preds], train["mass"])
mae_pipeline = mean_absolute_error(test["mass"], pipe.predict(test[preds]))
print(mae_pipeline)
print(mae_pipeline, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)
```
:::
:::
:::

The two objects are the same idea with different spelling. A recipe plus a
workflow, or a `ColumnTransformer` inside a `Pipeline`: in both, `fit()` sees
only the training rows, every fitted quantity is stored inside the object, and
applying it to new data cannot consult that data. You get the leak-free
behaviour because it is the only behaviour available, not because you
remembered.

## Task 3 — The scoreboard

Collect every MAE you have computed into one table, in the order you produced
them, and write the one sentence it supports.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tibble(
  pipeline = c("baseline: predict the training mean",
               "leak 1: scaled on all rows",
               "leak 2: mean-imputed on all rows",
               "leak 3: imputation model saw the outcome",
               "leak-free pipeline (recipes)"),
  MAE = c(mae_baseline, mae_scale_leak, mae_imp_leak, ______, mae_pipeline)
) |>
  mutate(vs_baseline = round(100 * MAE / mae_baseline))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

tibble(
  pipeline = c("baseline: predict the training mean",

               "leak 3: imputation model saw the outcome",
               "leak-free pipeline (recipes)"),
  MAE = c(mae_baseline, mae_scale_leak, mae_imp_leak, mae_impmodel_leak, mae_pipeline)
) |>

## Worked answer
```{python}
scoreboard = pd.DataFrame({
    "pipeline": ["baseline: predict the training mean",
                 "leak 1: scaled on all rows",
                 "leak 2: mean-imputed on all rows",
                 "leak 3: imputation model saw the outcome",
                 "leak-free pipeline (sklearn)"],
    "MAE": [mae_baseline, mae_scale_leak, mae_imp_leak, mae_impmodel_leak, mae_pipeline],
})
scoreboard["vs_baseline"] = (100 * scoreboard["MAE"] / mae_baseline).round()
print(scoreboard)
```
:::
:::
:::

The R and Python numbers will not match each other, because `set.seed(42)` and
`random_state=42` choose different rows — the same point Day 1 made in
@sec-pipeline. Within a language, the ordering is what matters.

## Reflection

1. Leak 3 produced the best MAE in your table. If a colleague showed you that
   model and that number, what would you ask for, and what would you expect to
   see in the answer?
2. Cross-validation repeats the split many times. Does putting your
   preprocessing inside a workflow or a `Pipeline` matter more or less once you
   are cross-validating, and why?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (R with seed 42, Python with `random_state=42`; the two
differ because the splits differ). Baseline MAE 5.5–5.9 BMI units. Leak 1: the
two MAEs are identical to within 1e-15 — if a student reports a difference in
the third decimal, they have changed the imputation or the split as well.
Leak 2: a difference of 0.0001–0.001, sign varying with the seed. Leak 3: leaky
3.7–4.4 against an honest 4.5–4.9; over sixty seeds the gap ran from 0.32 to
0.83 and the leaky version won every time. The leak-free pipeline reproduces
the honest number to the last digit — 4.46 in R and 4.92 in Python here, about
80–85% of the baseline — which is the point of Task 2: it is the same
arithmetic, with no opportunity to get the order wrong.

**The teaching line.** Resist the urge to tidy this into "leakage inflates
performance". Two of the three leaks did not, and students who have seen that
remember the real rule — information, not code order — rather than a
superstition about the sequence of lines.

**Reflection 1.** Ask for the preprocessing code, not the model. Specifically:
was any step fitted before the split, and did any step have access to the
outcome column? A single-number answer ("we used mean imputation") is not
enough; the question is what the imputer was fitted on.

**Reflection 2.** More. With one split you can audit the order by reading ten
lines. With ten-fold cross-validation the preprocessing has to be refitted
inside every fold, which is tedious to do by hand and automatic inside a
workflow — this is the usual reason leakage survives into published work.

**Common failures.** (1) Reusing `train_means` from Leak 1 inside Task 1 and
getting identical numbers — the variable name is the same on purpose, so make
them re-read. (2) In Python, `SimpleImputer` fitted on `dia[preds]` but applied
to a frame whose columns are in a different order. (3) `last_fit()` given a
recipe declared on `dia` rather than `train`: it still works, because
`last_fit()` re-estimates the steps on the training half, and that is worth
saying out loud rather than marking wrong.

**Timing.** Leak 1 and Leak 3 are the two that must happen. If you are short,
set Task 1 as reading, give them the difference, and spend the time on the
scoreboard.
:::
:::

## Stretch

The extra challenge from the original course material, rebuilt as a sequence
you can stop at any point. Use the same split throughout and add a row to your
scoreboard each time.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Does a better imputer help?
Swap `step_impute_mean()` for `step_impute_median()`, then for
`step_impute_bag()` — or in Python, `SimpleImputer(strategy="median")` and
`KNNImputer()`. Keep everything else identical. Report the MAEs. The honest
answer, which you should check rather than assume, is that it makes very little
difference, and knowing that is worth more than a tenth of a BMI unit.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Feature engineering inside the pipeline
Add `step_log(glucose)` or a banded age variable (`step_cut()` then
`step_dummy()`; `pd.cut()` then `OneHotEncoder`). Does the extra complexity
earn its place against the four-predictor model? Answer it with a table rather
than an impression.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — Build a leak you cannot see
Add twenty columns of pure random noise to the data. Choose the five most
correlated with `mass` **using all the rows**, fit on those five, and evaluate.
Then do the selection on the training rows only. One of the two beats the
baseline and neither should. Feature selection is a fitted step, and it is the
leak that is hardest to spot in somebody else's code.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can build a preprocessing pipeline whose fitted quantities
come from the training rows alone, in either language, and that you have
measured what three different leaks cost on one dataset.

**Cannot:** that a leak-free single split is a good estimate of anything. The
whole day has rested on one arbitrary 80/20 partition of 755 patients, which is
exactly what @sec-resampling then takes apart.
